newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Building rush swamps Tirana's green spaces.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Building rush swamps Tirana's green spaces.

text.p: The green spaces that once provided relief from the dusty summer heat of Albania's capital have been swamped by apartment blocks and cafes in the race for riches that followed the end of communist rule.
The banks of the Lana river are crammed with new structures built with more concern for speed than style, and construction has soared in the lawlessness of the past five months.
New apartment blocks are springing up to meet housing demand not met under communist rule, and those who cannot afford to move are building shaky-looking extensions.

The Youth Park adjoining the main Martyrs of the Nation Boulevard, once a popular trysting place for young couples, has been haphazardly concreted over. Many cafes were thrown up so quickly that trees are still sprouting from their roofs.
Pandeli Topalli of the Tirana regional environmental agency said of the more than 100 cafes in the park's three hectares (7.4 acres) only a handful had been correctly licensed by his office.
"The people who built them had the support of top officials and there was nothing we could do," he said.
"In Albania it was a kind of malady after the collapse of communism. Everyone wanted to become rich. People did everything they could without any thought for the future."
Tirana residents say their children have no place to play, and complain of dust from building sites and traffic congestion from private cars which were banned under communist rule.

The only green space remaining for the city's more than 400,000 residents is a lakeside park behind the university but this too has been reduced by encroaching development. Police now patrol the park to deter builders.
CONSTRUCTION STRAINING INFRASTRUCTURE

The construction is straining the city's already limited infrastructure. An estimated 60 percent of mains water leaks from ancient pipes and many homes have water for only a limited period three times a day. Others have none.

Topalli said Japanese government experts helped complete the first stage of a scheme to improve the sewage system but riots which followed the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes prevented them from returning in May as planned.

Tirana's outdoor cafes started as mobile kiosks under a policy to provide employment by boosting small businesses which spiralled out of control as more and more appeared, many of them unlicensed, and existing ones started putting down permanent foundations and adding upper storeys.

"The city government did it because they had no alternatives to offer. The local politicians could only see as far ahead as the next local elections, when they hoped to be re-elected," said Arjan Gace, forestry department director at the Committee of Environmental Preservation and Protection.
"They estimated each kiosk represented 10-12 people either working there or in their families, all potential votes."
The new cafes are packed in early evening as Tirana residents take their traditional stroll along the city's tree-lined boulevards.

Bar West, a popular haunt of journalists and politicians, offers marble-topped tables, stylish decor and air conditioning, as well as bullet holes left by gunmen who paid a warning visit on the first day of the state of emergency.
Normal life has started returning after five months of violence triggered by the collapse of the pyramid schemes that wiped out thousands of people's life savings in Europe's poorest country.
Cafe owners are hoping for an upturn in business following the lifting of a night-time curfew on July 24, though security worries still keep many people at home.
Two cafes on the Martyrs of the Nation Boulevard were destroyed by an explosion in the early hours of July 22 which police blamed on business rivalry.
ENVIRONMENTAL DAMAGE SPREADS TO OTHER AREAS

Environmental damage is not confined to Tirana. Outside the capital ancient forest in the mountainous northeast, home to wildlife such as bears and wolves, is under threat from logging, particularly close to roads.
Gace said former miners who lost their jobs when chrome, copper and nickel mines were shut down as uneconomic had turned to cutting wood for the construction industry as the only way to earn money.
The forestry department is issuing licences for selective logging which would allow the forest to return, but many small operators lack the equipment or skill to do the job properly.

Topalli said timber exports allowed after the end of communist rule were now banned, but added that destruction of the forest was not a new problem. Enver Hoxha's isolationist communist government tunnelled into the mountains and studded the countryside with hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers.
Since the looting of arms depots in March, lakes are under threat from fishermen who have discovered dynamite as an effective but ecologically devastating means of catching fish.

Topalli said other concerns raised by the long-isolated country's efforts to establish a market economy ranged from Italian companies setting up tanneries supplying their leather industry to benefit from low labour costs, to haphazard holiday developments along the coast.
"On the one hand, we need to control this kind of thing but then we're criticised for not permitting development," he said.
